a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
a.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules. Scanning the cloud service is the provider's responsibility under VDR-CSO-DET, and agencies should not attempt to scan it themselves. The agency scans what it operates: client software, agency-hosted components of a hybrid system, and any code the agency deploys into the service.

b.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules. Tool selection for the service is the provider's. VER-RPT-VDT sets what the provider must report about each detected vulnerability, and that is what determines how usable the reports are in agency tooling.

c.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules. VER-AGM-RVR expects agencies to review provider vulnerability reports at intervals commensurate with the risk posture in their Authorization to Operate, and providers report at least monthly under VER-TFR-MHR. Decide who performs this review and what threshold prompts agency action.

d.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Track vulnerabilities the provider has accepted.
d.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules. Remediation within the service is the provider's obligation under VDR-CSO-RES. What the agency must track is what the provider does not fix: under VER-TFR-MAV any vulnerability not fully mitigated or remediated within 192 days of evaluation is categorized as an accepted vulnerability, and those become risks the agency's Authorizing Official is carrying. VER-AGM-MAP expects agencies to use provider vulnerability information to maintain their own Plans of Action and Milestones.
d.notes: Accepted vulnerabilities are the clearest example of risk that transfers to the agency without any agency action. Ensure the AO sees the accepted vulnerability list, not only the summary of what was remediated.

e.agency_actions: Identify who receives vulnerability information.
e.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules. Where several agency systems use the same cloud service, share provider vulnerability reporting across them rather than having each track it separately.

f.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules. This applies to the provider's detection capability, which VDR-CSO-DET requires to be systematic, persistent, and prompt.

Check that boundary against the way the agency actually uses the service.

_.agency_actions: Respond to findings from assessments, monitoring, and audits.
_.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules. For findings in the cloud service the agency's options are limited: accept the risk, mitigate through configuration or compensating controls, raise it with the provider, or stop using the service for the affected data. VER-AGM-MAP expects agencies to carry relevant provider vulnerability information into their own Plans of Action and Milestones. Where a concern is serious enough that it would likely lead to rescinding the ATO, AGU-USE-NFC requires the agency to notify FedRAMP, and AGU-USE-NPC recommends notifying the provider as well.

This feeds the contingency planning under CP-02 a and the availability expectations recorded under SC-05.

_.agency_actions: Review Cloud Service documentation. Restrict agency access to administrative interfaces.
_.fedramp_guidance: Separation of user-facing functionality from system management functionality is an architectural property of the cloud service and will be implemented by the CSP. The agency remains responsible for ensuring agency administrators reach management functions through separate privileged accounts and roles rather than their general business-user accounts (see AC-06(02) and AC-02(07)). Document any agency-applied configuration that controls who can reach administrative interfaces, including conditional access or network restrictions enforced through the agency IdP.
_.notes: SC-02 is concerned with architecture, not account management. If the cloud service presents administrative functions inline within the same interface used by business users, the agency generally cannot remediate this through configuration and should document it as a risk for AO acceptance.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Confirm the tenancy model meets agency isolation requirements.
_.fedramp_guidance: Preventing unauthorized or unintended information transfer via shared resources — object reuse, memory and storage residue, and isolation between tenants — is implemented by the CSP and its underlying IaaS/PaaS provider.
_.notes: There is little the agency can do to remediate weak resource isolation through configuration. If the shared-tenancy model is insufficient for the use case, the realistic options are AO risk acceptance, a dedicated or government-community deployment if the provider offers one, or restricting which data types are placed in the service. Document whichever path is chosen.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Define the availability the agency information system requires.
a.fedramp_guidance: In a Rev5 package the types of denial-of-service events the service addresses, and whether their effects are prevented or only limited, are provider-assigned control parameters under FRC-CSF-ACP; FedRAMP assigns no values for this control. Compare the provider's determination against the availability the agency information system actually needs. CDS-CSO-AVR applies to either package type and requires the provider to maintain a web service showing current and historical availability of core services over at least the past 30 days, including availability incidents, that remains reachable even when the service itself is not — use it to see how the service has performed rather than only how it is designed.
a.notes: IVV-CSF-AIA and IVV-CSF-MCA are Rev5-only rules. In a Rev5 package SC-05 is not in the Class C mandatory annual assessment set, so it falls under the three-year ceiling and independent assessment evidence for this control may be up to three years old. The availability reporting required by CDS-CSO-AVR applies to either package type and is the better source for how the service performs today.

b.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Configure any agency-controlled quota, rate limit, or connection settings.
b.fedramp_guidance: The controls that achieve the denial-of-service objective — upstream filtering, rate limiting, capacity and bandwidth management, and automatic scaling — are implemented by the CSP and its underlying infrastructure provider. Review the Secure Configuration Guide for any tenant-level quota, rate limit, or session and connection settings the agency controls; AGU-USE-RSG requires agencies to review provider Secure Configuration Guides and configure relevant security settings.
b.notes: An agency consuming the service cannot add denial-of-service protection to it. If the provider’s protections do not meet the agency’s availability needs, the realistic paths are AO risk acceptance or contingency planning for periods of unavailability under the CP family, not remediation. Agencies are encouraged to work with CSPs since additional availability can usually be achieved at an additional cost.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Identify the interfaces between the agency information system and the cloud service.
a.fedramp_guidance: The managed interfaces inside the cloud service, and the monitoring and control applied at them, are implemented by the CSP. MAS-CSO-FLO applies to either package type and requires providers to identify, document, and explain the information flows for every information resource in the offering — that documentation is where the service boundary becomes visible. The agency remains responsible for the interfaces it operates: connections from agency networks and endpoints, and any agency system that exchanges data with the service.

b.fedramp_guidance: Separation of publicly accessible components from internal networks is an architectural property of the cloud service and is implemented by the CSP. Do not expect to find traditional subnetworks: FedRAMP Rev5 Controls Guidance for SC-07 (b) allows this to be met by any technical capability or complement of capabilities that ensures logical separation, provided traffic cannot traverse from publicly accessible components to internal networks without inspection and authorization. That guidance is Rev5-specific and has no counterpart in a 20x package.

c.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Document how the agency information system connects to the cloud service.
c.fedramp_guidance: The service's own external connections are managed by the CSP. For the agency information system this control is about the path the agency uses to reach the service: document the managed interface at the agency end — network egress, inspection points, or a proxy or CASB — and treat the service as an External System Service under SA-09 rather than an extension of the agency network. Boundary protection at the agency end is normally inherited from agency enterprise network systems; reference those controls rather than restating them here.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Limit the number of agency integration points to the service.
_.fedramp_guidance: The number of external network connections to the cloud service is controlled by the CSP. The agency's equivalent responsibility is the number of distinct integrations it creates — API clients, data feeds, single sign-on connections, and administrative access paths — each of which is a connection the agency must document and monitor. Keeping that set small and enumerated is what makes the rest of the SC-07 enhancements tractable.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Managed interfaces for external telecommunications services, the traffic flow policy, and control plane protections are implemented by the CSP and its underlying infrastructure provider. Review the information flow documentation required by MAS-CSO-FLO, which applies to either package type. Where the agency operates its own interface to the service, the traffic flow policy exceptions in part (d) and the review frequency in part (e) are agency-determined.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Restrict which agency networks and users can reach the tenant.
_.fedramp_guidance: Default-deny at the service's managed interfaces is implemented by the CSP. Where the service offers tenant-level network controls — address allowlisting, private connectivity, or conditional access by device or location — the agency configures them; AGU-USE-RSG requires agencies to review provider Secure Configuration Guides and configure relevant security settings. Document the resulting set of allowed paths.

_.agency_actions: Confirm agency endpoint and VPN configurations prevent split tunneling.
_.fedramp_guidance: This enhancement applies to the remote devices the agency uses to reach the cloud service, not to the service itself, and is normally satisfied by agency enterprise endpoint and VPN configuration. Reference the agency systems that provide it rather than restating their implementation here. Where agency users reach the service directly from the internet rather than through an agency-managed path, document that decision and the device and identity controls that apply instead.

_.agency_actions: Determine whether agency traffic to the service is routed through an authenticated proxy.
_.fedramp_guidance: Like SC-07 (07), this concerns the path from agency networks to the cloud service rather than the service's internal architecture. Where the agency routes user traffic through a proxy, secure web gateway, or CASB, that capability is normally inherited from agency enterprise network systems. The internal communications traffic in scope and the external networks it may reach are agency-determined.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Host-based boundary protection on the components that make up the cloud service is implemented by the CSP. In a Rev5 package the mechanisms used and the components they apply to are provider-assigned parameters under FRC-CSF-ACP. No Key Security Indicator maps to this enhancement, so a 20x package will not contain a directly corresponding entry. If the agency information system is a hybrid system leveraging some agency-operated components, the agency should complete this control for those components.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Preventing the service from entering an unsecure state when a boundary protection device fails is implemented by the CSP.
_.notes: Failing secure and remaining available pull in opposite directions. The provider's choice here shapes the availability the agency can expect, so read this alongside SC-05 rather than in isolation.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Configure the service to accept only encrypted connections.
_.fedramp_guidance: Protection of transmitted information is implemented by the CSP. Review the Secure Configuration Guide to identify any transmission settings the agency controls; AGU-USE-RSG requires agencies to review provider Secure Configuration Guides and configure relevant security settings. Document the applied configuration. This overlaps with AC-17(02) — if encrypted connections are documented there, reference that entry rather than repeating it.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package
_.fedramp_guidance: Cryptographic mechanisms protecting information in transit are implemented by the CSP. Follow the FedRAMP Cryptographic Module Use rules and review the module documentation supplied under CMU-CSO-CMD to confirm which modules protect transmitted federal customer data and whether they are CMVP-validated.
_.notes: Use of CMVP-validated cryptographic modules is a SHOULD at Class C under CMU-CSO-UVM, not a MUST — it is only mandatory at Class D. A Class C provider is required to document which modules it uses (CMU-CSO-CMD) but is not required to use validated ones. Agencies with a statutory or policy requirement for FIPS-validated cryptography must verify this directly rather than inferring it from certification status.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Determine the session inactivity period for agency users.
_.fedramp_guidance: Termination of a connection at the end of a session or after inactivity is implemented by the CSP. In a Rev5 package the time period is a provider-assigned parameter under FRC-CSF-ACP. Where the service exposes a configurable idle or session timeout for the agency tenant, the agency sets it — review the Secure Configuration Guide and document the applied value. This overlaps with AC-12; if the timeout is recorded there, reference that entry rather than repeating it.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Determine whether agency-managed keys are required.
_.fedramp_guidance: Key establishment and management for the cloud service is implemented by the CSP. In a Rev5 package the key management requirements are provider-assigned parameters under FRC-CSF-ACP. The FedRAMP Cryptographic Module Use rules apply to either package type — review the module documentation supplied under CMU-CSO-CMD. Where the service offers customer-managed or agency-supplied keys, the agency decides whether to use that option and takes on the key lifecycle responsibilities that come with it.
_.notes: Electing to manage keys moves real operational risk to the agency — key loss can render data unrecoverable in ways the provider cannot remedy. Document the recovery path before choosing agency-managed keys.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
a.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Cryptographic Module Use rules. CMU-CSO-CMD requires providers to document the cryptographic modules used in each service where cryptography protects federal customer data, including whether each module is validated under the NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program. Review this documentation to identify which cryptographic uses the provider has determined for the service.
a.notes: Use of CMVP-validated cryptographic modules is a SHOULD at Class C under CMU-CSO-UVM, not a MUST — it is only mandatory at Class D. A Class C provider is required to document which modules it uses (CMU-CSO-CMD) but is not required to use validated ones. Agencies with a statutory or policy requirement for FIPS-validated cryptography must verify this directly rather than inferring it from certification status.

b.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Verify agency tenant cryptographic settings.
b.fedramp_guidance: Implementation is handled by the CSP. CMU-CSO-CAT states providers SHOULD configure agency tenants by default to use validated cryptographic modules where available — verify the applied default rather than assuming it, and document any agency-selected cryptographic settings.

a.agency_actions: Determine whether the service provides collaborative computing capabilities, and define any permitted exceptions.
a.fedramp_guidance: This control applies only where the cloud service provides collaborative computing capabilities such as audio or video conferencing, screen sharing, or remote desktop. Where it does, the exceptions under which remote activation is permitted are agency-determined and should align with existing agency policy rather than a new one written for this system.
a.notes: Many services in scope for this document have no collaborative computing capability at all. Record that determination explicitly rather than leaving the control unaddressed.

b.fedramp_guidance: The explicit indication of use — an active-camera or active-microphone indicator visible to the person at the device — is a property of the service's client software and of the endpoint operating system. It is implemented by the CSP and the device platform rather than configured by the agency.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Identify the certificate policy covering any certificates the agency supplies.
a.fedramp_guidance: Certificates for the cloud service's own endpoints are obtained and managed by the CSP. Where the agency supplies a certificate — for a custom domain, for client authentication, or for signing single sign-on assertions — the agency issues it under an approved agency certificate policy or obtains it from an approved service provider.

b.agency_actions: Confirm only approved trust anchors are present in agency-managed trust stores.
b.fedramp_guidance: Trust stores inside the cloud service are managed by the CSP. The agency is responsible for the trust stores it manages on agency endpoints and in agency systems that connect to the service. This is normally inherited from agency enterprise device management; reference those controls rather than restating them here.

a.agency_actions: Define acceptable and unacceptable mobile code and mobile code technologies.
a.fedramp_guidance: Cloud services delivered through a browser depend on mobile code — JavaScript and WebAssembly in particular — so a blanket prohibition is not workable for a system of this kind. Define acceptability in terms of where code originates and how it is delivered rather than by technology alone, and align the definition with existing agency policy instead of writing a parallel one for this system.

b.fedramp_guidance: Authorization, monitoring, and control of mobile code within the service is implemented by the CSP through its development and supply chain processes. Enforcement at the agency end — browser policy, extension allowlisting, and content restrictions — is normally inherited from agency enterprise endpoint systems.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Identify who operates the domain names used to reach the service.
a.fedramp_guidance: Origin authentication and integrity artifacts for the service's own authoritative name resolution are implemented by the CSP. Where the agency information system is reached through an agency-owned domain name, the agency operates that zone and is responsible for signing it.

b.fedramp_guidance: The chain of trust between parent and child zones is maintained by whoever operates each zone. Where the agency delegates a subdomain to the cloud service, the agency is responsible for publishing the delegation records that allow resolvers to verify the child zone.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Validation of name resolution responses received by the cloud service is implemented by the CSP. The resolvers agency endpoints use to reach the service are normally an agency enterprise service; reference the agency systems that provide validating resolution rather than restating them here.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Fault tolerance and internal and external role separation for the name resolution service are implemented by the CSP and its underlying infrastructure provider.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Session authenticity — session token generation and binding, transport session integrity, and protection against session fixation and hijacking — is implemented by the CSP. Review the Secure Configuration Guide for any session handling settings exposed to the agency tenant. This is closely tied to SC-08; where transport protection is already documented there, reference that entry rather than repeating it.

_.agency_actions: Identify the agency information that will be stored in the service and the protection it requires. Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: The agency determines what information it places in the service and the confidentiality and integrity protection that information requires, consistent with the categorization assigned under RA-02. Protection at rest is implemented by the CSP. Review the Secure Configuration Guide for any storage, retention, or encryption settings the agency controls.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package
_.fedramp_guidance: Cryptographic mechanisms protecting information at rest are implemented by the CSP. Follow the FedRAMP Cryptographic Module Use rules and review the module documentation supplied under CMU-CSO-CMD to confirm which modules protect stored federal customer data and whether they are CMVP-validated. Verify that the coverage extends to backups as well as primary storage.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Separate execution domains for executing processes are provided by the compute platform underlying the cloud service and are implemented by the CSP. This is closely related to SC-04; where the tenancy and isolation model is already documented there, reference that entry rather than repeating it.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Clock synchronization within and between the components of the cloud service is implemented by the CSP. The agency's practical interest is log correlation: confirm that timestamps in the logs the agency receives from the service can be reliably correlated with timestamps produced by agency systems, and record the time zone and format the service uses. Related to AU-08.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: In a Rev5 package the authoritative time source, the frequency of comparison, and the time difference that triggers resynchronization are provider-assigned parameters under FRC-CSF-ACP; review them where the agency has log correlation or non-repudiation requirements that depend on clock accuracy. No Key Security Indicator maps to this enhancement, so a 20x package will not contain a directly corresponding entry.

a.agency_actions: Document system and information integrity policy control decisions that are specific to this information system
a.fedramp_guidance: Some policies and procedures will be inherited from other agency systems and/or cloud systems. You do not need to repeat that information here.

b.fedramp_guidance: Determine the agency role or personnel accountable for the policies and procedures in this control family. This is an agency position and should not be assigned to the cloud service provider. This person or role may not be responsible for all implementation, monitoring, or enforcement of the controls but should be accountable to leadership for compliance with all relevant policies and procedures.

c.fedramp_guidance: How often and by whom will the policies and procedures in this control family be reviewed? Provide a broad policy here (e.g. “Policies and procedures will be reviewed at least annually or in response to any relevant incidents or changes”) and then provide more detailed additional review requirements for specific controls as needed.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
a.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules. Identifying and correcting flaws in the cloud service is the provider's responsibility under VDR-CSO-DET and VDR-CSO-RES. The agency's part is receiving the reports and acting where they affect it; this overlaps with RA-05 c, so record the review process once and reference it.

b.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules. Testing updates before installation is the provider's responsibility. Where the service offers a preview or early-release channel, the agency may choose to validate changes against its own configuration before they reach production users.

c.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules. Update timelines within the service are the provider's. VER-TFR-MAV sets the outer bound the agency should care about: anything not fully mitigated or remediated within 192 days of evaluation is categorized as an accepted vulnerability.

d.agency_actions: Incorporate provider flaw remediation into the agency configuration management process.
d.fedramp_guidance: Provider updates are changes to the agency information system even though the agency does not make them. The configuration management process defined under CM-03 should account for them, including the documentation review after provider-side changes that CM-02 b requires.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules. Automated determination of remediation status is the provider's. What reaches the agency is the periodic reporting required under VER-RPT-PER.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Measuring time to remediate within the service is the provider's. The benchmark the agency can hold to is VER-TFR-MAV: 192 days from evaluation, after which an unremediated vulnerability is categorized as accepted. No Key Security Indicator maps to this enhancement, so a 20x package will not contain a directly corresponding entry.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
a.fedramp_guidance: Malicious code protection within the cloud service is implemented by the CSP. Agency endpoints remain the agency's responsibility and are normally covered by enterprise endpoint protection; reference that rather than restating it. Where the service allows users to upload files, establish how uploads are scanned.

b.fedramp_guidance: Updating protection mechanisms within the service is the provider's responsibility. For agency endpoints this is inherited from enterprise endpoint management.

c.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Determine who receives malicious code alerts.
c.fedramp_guidance: Scan frequency and response actions within the service are the provider's to configure. The agency's decision is who is alerted when malicious code is found in agency content and what happens next; align that with the incident response plan under IR-08 a.

d.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
d.fedramp_guidance: False positives that quarantine legitimate agency content are an availability problem as much as a security one. Establish how the agency requests review of a quarantined item and how long that takes.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Define what the agency monitors in its own use of the service.
a.fedramp_guidance: Monitoring the cloud service for attacks is the provider's responsibility. The agency monitors its own use: authentication events, privilege changes, data export and sharing activity, and administrative actions. Review the Secure Configuration Guide for the log feeds the service exposes and route them into agency monitoring rather than reviewing them in the provider's console.

b.agency_actions: Define the techniques used to identify unauthorized use.
b.fedramp_guidance: In a cloud service, unauthorized use usually looks like a legitimate account behaving unusually rather than an intrusion. Anomalous data export, sharing to external recipients, and access from unexpected locations are the patterns worth building detections for.

c.fedramp_guidance: Placement of monitoring within the service is the provider's. The agency's equivalent decision is which of the available log streams to collect — collecting everything is rarely affordable and rarely useful.

d.agency_actions: Analyze detected events and anomalies.
d.fedramp_guidance: Analysis is normally performed by the agency security operations function using existing tooling. What is specific to this system is the context needed to interpret events: who the users are, which roles are privileged, and what normal data movement looks like.

e.agency_actions: Adjust the level of monitoring when risk changes.
e.fedramp_guidance: Provider-reported incidents and changes to the service are the triggers most specific to this system. A FedRAMP Reportable Incident affecting the provider is a reason to raise monitoring of agency activity in the service rather than to wait for the provider's final report.

f.agency_actions: Obtain a legal opinion regarding system monitoring activities.
f.fedramp_guidance: This is an agency legal function and is normally addressed agency-wide rather than per system. Monitoring use of a cloud service can raise questions an existing opinion did not consider, particularly where the provider processes data outside the agency's direct control.

g.agency_actions: Determine who receives system monitoring information, and when.
g.fedramp_guidance: Identify the recipients and the cadence. Include whoever reviews provider vulnerability and certification reporting, so that agency-side and provider-side observations are read together rather than separately.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Connecting individual intrusion detection tools into a system-wide capability is the provider's responsibility for the cloud service. No Key Security Indicator maps to this enhancement, so a 20x package will not contain a directly corresponding entry.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Real-time analysis within the service is the provider's. The agency's equivalent is its own SIEM; the practical question is whether the service's log feeds arrive quickly enough to support real-time analysis or only in batch.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Traffic monitoring at the service boundary is the provider's. Agency-side, the equivalent is monitoring traffic from agency networks to the service, normally inherited from enterprise network monitoring.

_.agency_actions: Determine which service alerts the agency acts on, and who receives them.
_.fedramp_guidance: Most cloud services can generate more alerts than an agency can action. Select the ones tied to agency risk — privilege escalation, external sharing, bulk export, improbable sign-in locations — and route them to a monitored destination rather than to an inbox.

_.fedramp_guidance: Correlation only works if timestamps line up; settle the time source and format questions raised under SC-45 before relying on it. No Key Security Indicator maps to this enhancement, so a 20x package will not contain a directly corresponding entry.

_.fedramp_guidance: Detecting covert exfiltration from the service is the provider's responsibility. The agency's realistic contribution is monitoring for bulk or unusual data egress performed through legitimate service features, which is how exfiltration from a SaaS platform normally happens. No Key Security Indicator maps to this enhancement, so a 20x package will not contain a directly corresponding entry.

If the agency information system is a hybrid system leveraging some agency operated components and some cloud service components then the agency should complete this control for the agency operated components. No Key Security Indicator maps to this enhancement.

a.agency_actions: Identify the external sources of security alerts and advisories for this system.
a.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Addressing FedRAMP Communication rules. Beyond the agency's usual sources, this system depends on provider communications: ongoing certification reporting, incident notification, and significant change notification. Confirm the agency is registered to receive them and that they arrive somewhere monitored.

b.agency_actions: Generate internal security alerts and advisories as needed.
b.fedramp_guidance: Where a provider advisory requires agency action — a configuration change, a credential rotation, a message to users — turn it into an internal alert rather than assuming recipients will act on the provider's notice.

c.agency_actions: Determine who receives security alerts, advisories, and directives.
c.fedramp_guidance: Include the roles accountable for the affected control families and the Access Control Officer designated under AC-02 b.

d.agency_actions: Implement security directives within the required time frames.
d.fedramp_guidance: Where a directive requires a change the agency cannot make because the capability sits with the provider, notify the issuing organization of the degree of noncompliance and record it as a risk. Where the shortfall is significant enough to threaten the Authorization to Operate, AGU-USE-NPC and AGU-USE-NFC require notifying the provider and FedRAMP.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
a.fedramp_guidance: Verifying the correct operation of security and privacy functions within the service is the provider's responsibility. No Key Security Indicator maps to this control, so a 20x package will not contain a directly corresponding entry.

b.fedramp_guidance: The trigger and frequency for verification are the provider's to determine.

c.fedramp_guidance: Determine whether the agency is notified when a provider verification test fails, or whether it would learn only through incident or certification reporting.

d.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
d.fedramp_guidance: The action taken when anomalies are discovered is the provider's decision, and it is the same fail-secure versus availability trade-off described under SC-07 (18).

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
a.fedramp_guidance: Integrity verification within the cloud service is implemented by the CSP. The agency's equivalent is detecting unauthorized change to the configuration it controls, described under CM-03 f.

b.fedramp_guidance: Response to detected integrity failures within the service is the provider's. The agency's concern is being told: confirm that an integrity failure affecting agency data would reach the agency as an incident notification.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: The frequency and triggers for integrity checks within the service are the provider's to determine.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Integrating integrity detection into incident response is the provider's responsibility for the service. The agency's equivalent integration is between the service's alerts and the incident response plan developed under IR-08 a.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package. Confirm DMARC configuration where the service sends email using an agency domain.
a.fedramp_guidance: Spam protection within the service is implemented by the CSP. FedRAMP guidance for SI-08 is specific where the service sends email on behalf of the government: the provider should implement DMARC on the sending domain in line with DHS Binding Operational Directive 18-01, with policy=reject and the rua parameter including reports@dmarc.cyber.dhs.gov, and should document the FROM: domains used. Confirm this before allowing the service to send mail using an agency domain.
a.notes: A service sending mail from an agency domain without a correct DMARC record puts the agency's domain reputation at risk, not just the service's. This is one of the few SI controls where an agency configuration decision has consequences outside the system.

b.fedramp_guidance: Updating spam protection mechanisms is the provider's responsibility.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Automatic updating of spam protection mechanisms is the provider's responsibility.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Input validation is implemented by the CSP as part of its development process. Where the agency builds extensions, scripts, or integrations that submit data to the service, those are agency code and the agency validates their inputs.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
a.fedramp_guidance: Error message content is determined by the CSP. Where the agency configures custom error pages or messages, keep system detail out of them.

b.fedramp_guidance: Restricting who sees detailed errors is the provider's responsibility. Where the service exposes diagnostic or debug output to agency administrators, treat access to it as privileged and cover it under AC-06.

_.agency_actions: Manage and retain information within the system and information output from the system
_.fedramp_guidance: Retention is an agency determination driven by records schedules and legal obligations, not by the service's defaults. Review the Secure Configuration Guide for retention, versioning, and deletion settings, and confirm the service can hold data for as long as the schedule requires and delete it when the schedule says to. Where the service cannot express the agency's retention rules, the agency must export the records and manage them elsewhere.
_.notes: Retention fails in two directions and cloud services fail at both ends: keeping data longer than the schedule permits, and deleting it sooner than the schedule allows. Check both against the applicable records schedule rather than only the first.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Memory protection is a property of the platform underlying the cloud service and is implemented by the CSP. This is closely related to SC-39; where process isolation is documented there, reference that entry rather than repeating it.

a.agency_actions: Document supply chain risk management control decisions that are specific to this information system
a.fedramp_guidance: Some policies and procedures will be inherited from other agency systems and/or cloud systems. You do not need to repeat that information here.

b.fedramp_guidance: Determine the agency role or personnel accountable for the policies and procedures in this control family. This is an agency position and should not be assigned to the cloud service provider. This person or role may not be responsible for all implementation, monitoring, or enforcement of the controls but should be accountable to leadership for compliance with all relevant policies and procedures.

c.fedramp_guidance: How often and by whom will the policies and procedures in this control family be reviewed? Provide a broad policy here (e.g. “Policies and procedures will be reviewed at least annually or in response to any relevant incidents or changes”) and then provide more detailed additional review requirements for specific controls as needed.

a.agency_actions: Determine whether the agency-wide supply chain risk management plan covers this system, or whether system-specific content is needed.
a.fedramp_guidance: An agency information system built on a cloud service has no hardware supply chain of its own — its supply chain is the cloud service and the third-party resources that service depends on. MAS-CSO-TPR requires providers to identify the third-party information resources within the offering, and that inventory is the agency's view of the supply chain it is accepting. Reference the agency-wide plan and record only what is specific to this system.

b.agency_actions: Determine the frequency for reviewing and updating the supply chain risk management plan.
b.fedramp_guidance: Determine the frequency or triggers that will require the plan to be reviewed. A change in the provider's third-party dependencies is the trigger specific to this system, and it surfaces through the Ongoing Certification Report rather than through agency observation.

c.agency_actions: Protect the supply chain risk management plan from unauthorized disclosure and modification.
c.fedramp_guidance: Where the plan is agency-wide this is inherited along with it. Where system-specific content has been added, apply the same handling as the plans under PL-02 e.

_.agency_actions: Identify the agency supply chain risk management team supporting this system.
_.fedramp_guidance: This is normally an existing agency function rather than a team stood up for one system. Identify who performs it and how this system's provider dependencies reach them.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
a.fedramp_guidance: Identifying and addressing weaknesses in the cloud service's supply chain is the provider's responsibility. FedRAMP guidance for SR-03 requires the provider to document and maintain supply chain custody, including replacement devices, so that device integrity is established before anything is introduced to the boundary. The agency's own process applies to components it introduces itself.

b.fedramp_guidance: The controls protecting the service against supply chain risk are the provider's. For the agency, the principal supply chain control available is the FedRAMP Certification itself — the verified chain of trust described in the front matter of this document. Where the agency adds integrations or client software, those become agency supply chain elements and need controls of their own.

c.agency_actions: Document the supply chain processes and controls that apply to this system.
c.fedramp_guidance: Record these in the agency SSP or the supply chain risk management plan, whichever the agency uses. Where the answer is that the risk is accepted through the FedRAMP Certification, state that explicitly rather than leaving the control unaddressed.

_.agency_actions: Document the acquisition approach used to procure the cloud service.
_.fedramp_guidance: Procuring a FedRAMP Certified offering is itself the principal acquisition control for this system. Record the vehicle used and the contract terms that bear on security — notification obligations, data location, data return and deletion on exit, and the right to receive ongoing certification reporting.

_.agency_actions: Determine the frequency for assessing supply chain risk associated with the provider.
_.fedramp_guidance: The provider is reassessed continuously through FedRAMP rather than by the agency. Align the agency's review with the Ongoing Certification Report, which arrives every three months under CCM-OCR-AVL and which CCM-AGM-ROR requires agencies to review. AGU-USE-RIR adds that agencies should consider the provider's third-party information resources during initial and ongoing authorization activities.

_.agency_actions: Confirm the notification path for supply chain compromises affecting the service.
_.fedramp_guidance: Follow the FedRAMP Incident Evaluation and Communication rules. Providers must evaluate incidents for FedRAMP reportability under IEC-CSO-EFR and issue initial, ongoing, and final incident reports to affected parties. The agency's task is to ensure those reports reach a monitored destination and that someone is accountable for acting on them, rather than to negotiate a separate notification agreement.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Physical inspection of components is the provider's responsibility and is not something an agency consuming a cloud service can perform. The agency's equivalent is detecting unauthorized change in what it does control — the configuration drift monitoring described under CM-03 f serves this purpose better than any inspection regime.

a.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
a.fedramp_guidance: Anti-counterfeit policy applies to physical components and is the provider's responsibility for the cloud service. Where the agency information system includes agency-operated hardware, the agency's existing anti-counterfeit policy applies to those components.

b.fedramp_guidance: Reporting counterfeit components is the provider's responsibility for the service. Where the agency detects a counterfeit among its own components, report through the agency's existing process.

_.agency_actions: Review the CSP Cybersecurity Education training plan
_.fedramp_guidance: Determine the effectiveness and frequency of anti-counterfeit training, and how successful the users complete the training.

_.agency_actions: Review Certification Package.
_.fedramp_guidance: Generally this requirement will be implemented by the CSP. If the agency information system is a hybrid system leveraging some agency operated components and some cloud service components then the agency should complete this control for the agency operated components.

_.agency_actions: Determine how agency data and documentation are disposed of at the end of the service relationship.
_.fedramp_guidance: The provider disposes of its own components. The agency's concern is its data: confirm what happens to agency data when the subscription ends, how quickly it is removed, and what evidence of removal the provider supplies. This belongs in the contract and is closely related to the sanitization decisions recorded under MP-06 a.
